titulo: The map of the cases: What is a case

aula.objetivo: Understand what cases are, see the map of the six cases, and recognise which case appears, and why, in sentences you already know.

blocos.texto: (or: the case of the action — and the one question that settles everything: is it animate?)

blocos.explicacao: A scene you have lived (or will). Picture it. You are in Russia. You have studied the alphabet, nouns, adjectives, verbs in the present, past and future. You feel confident. You walk into a shop, point at something and say: — Я ви́жу кни́га. The shop assistant understands, but winces. She repeats it, correcting you: — Я ви́жу кни́гу. You look again. It is the same word, кни́га, but now it ends in -у, not -а. You think: "Why? I learned that кни́га is feminine. Why did the ending change?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the accusative case. It sounds complicated, but it is not. Five minutes of careful reading will save you years of false immersion. What English already does. English has almost no cases, but it keeps a trace of this one in its pronouns. You say "I see him", never "I see he". You say "She loves me", never "She loves I". "Him", "her", "me", "us", "them", "whom" are the accusative (the object form) of he, she, I, we, they, who. Russian does the same with pronouns (я → меня, он → его), and, unlike English, it does it with nouns too. The case of action. The accusative is the case of the thing the action is done to. When you say "I read the book", "the book" is the object of the action. In English you know it is the object only because of word order (it comes after the verb). Russian lets the ending carry that job, which is why the word order can be freer. This object needs a special mark in Russian. That mark is the accusative case.

blocos.titulo: Animate and inanimate: who "has a soul"
blocos.explicacao: The Russian view: who has a soul? Now comes the most fascinating part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. In Russian grammar, only people and animals "have a soul" (this is the traditional teaching image; grammarians call it animate versus inanimate). People have a soul. Animals have a soul. Objects don't. Plants don't. Ideas don't. A house has no soul. A stone has no soul. But a friend does. A dog does. A child does. What does this have to do with grammar? Everything. Because only those with a soul get special treatment in the accusative. Only they change form when they are the object of the action. I'll explain with the magic question: does the word have a soul? If YES → it is "animate" and gets a special mark in the accusative (in the masculine). If NO → it is "inanimate" and does not change in the accusative (in the masculine). Examples: Does Дом (house) have a soul? No. A house is an object, so it does not change in the accusative. Стол (table)? No, so it does not change. Друг (friend)? Yes, a person, so it changes in the accusative. Студент (student)? Yes, a person, so it changes. Собака (dog)? Yes, an animal. But wait: «собака» is feminine, and for the feminine the rule is different. We will get there. Keep this question in your head. It will solve 90% of your accusative mistakes. The single rule that solves it all. Before the details, here is the rule in one sentence. Memorise it: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES. It makes no difference whether it has a soul or not. Always. MASCULINE: DEPENDS ON THE SOUL. If it has a soul, it changes. If not, it does not change. NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. It is neuter, by nature. That is all. Three lines. You have just learned the accusative of nouns. Now the details.

The FEMININE: it always changes. The feminine is the easiest because it is consistent. It always changes, whether it has a soul or not. Feminine ending in -А → becomes -У. You drop the -а and put -у. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Я → becomes -Ю. You drop the -я and put -ю. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Ь → DOES NOT CHANGE. The feminine in -ь stays the same as the nominative. Attention: how do you know whether a feminine word will change? Look at the ending. Ends in -а → changes to -у. Ends in -я → changes to -ю. Ends in -ь → no change. And the soul? For the feminine it does not matter. The rule is always the same, with a soul or without. That is why the feminine is the easiest.

blocos.titulo: Case: the function of a word in the sentence
blocos.explicacao: In English, the function of a word shows in word order and prepositions: «the dog bit the man» is not «the man bit the dog». In Russian, the function shows in the ending: the word changes its ending, and each ending is a case. There are six cases. In «Мама читает книгу», «мама» is who does the action (nominative) and «книгу» is what receives the action (accusative). You have already used four of the six cases without knowing their names; now they get names.
blocos.comparacao: English does not change its nouns, but it does change its pronouns: «I / me», «he / him». Russian does this with every word.

tabela.question: Кто? Что?
tabela.funcao: who does it; the dictionary form

tabela.question: Кому? Чему?
tabela.funcao: to whom, for whom (coming up next)

tabela.question: Кем? Чем?
tabela.funcao: with whom, by means of (coming up next)

erros.motivo: The direct object goes into the accusative.

blocos.enunciado: Say «Мама читает книгу.» Then swap «мама» and «книга» for other words and adjust the endings.
Write one sentence with «У меня нет», one with «в» + a place and one with «читаю» + an object.
